fields.features_heading: What Emergent Builds Into a DSAR Workflow
fields.features_subheading: Every request becomes one record that fills in as systems answer and reviewers sign off.
fields.feature_1:
A numbered record for every request

Emergent builds the request form and the database behind it from your prompt. Each request is saved with its number and the date it arrived, and it sits in a database you own.
fields.feature_2:
Due dates from the window you choose

Pick the response window for each privacy law your team works under, and the app sets the due date as each request arrives. An extension cannot be saved without a written reason.
fields.feature_3:
Searches across the systems that hold data

Emergent connects the app to the CRM and other systems holding customer data through their APIs. Each is searched by the requester's email, and matching records land on the request.
fields.feature_4:
An identity check before data moves

The app compares the name and email on each request with the customer record. A mismatch pauses the request for an analyst, who can ask the requester for more detail first.
fields.feature_5:
Alerts that leave the personal data behind

Owners get a Slack or email alert holding a request number and a link. The person's records stay in the database, and a task left open past its due date moves up to the privacy lead.
fields.feature_6:
The request app's code, in your GitHub

Export the full code to your GitHub repository on paid plans. Your security team can read how request files are stored and who can open them, the same way it reviews any other code.

fields.usecase_heading: Four Requests a Privacy Team Handles
fields.tab_content_1:
Request A-2041 collects 214 records from the CRM

A customer in Germany asks Orlenby Software for a copy of their data, and request A-2041 opens with a due date one month out. The app searches three systems by the customer's email. It finds 214 CRM records, 37 support tickets, and 18 invoices, and analyst Clothilde Thibodaux gets a link to review the package.
fields.tab_content_2:
Delete request D-0317 waits on one system owner

Polwhele Home Goods confirms a California shopper's request the day it arrives, and request D-0317 is due in 45 days. Owners of 4 systems get a delete task, and three confirm within a week. Ingmar Ferrabosco owns the email platform and has not replied. On day 7 he gets a reminder with the request number and a link.
fields.tab_content_3:
Until counsel approves, nothing goes to the former driver

A former driver asks Quillstead Freight for his data. Request E-0082 gathers his HR file, payroll records, and 412 emails that name him. Employment counsel Oskarine Caulfeild marks 9 pages that name other employees for redaction. The package stays locked until she approves it, and her note is saved to the request.
fields.tab_content_4:
Edwige gets each request with 5 days left

Every Monday, Edwige Tavistock opens the board of open requests at Vellichor Learning. It lists 23, sorted by due date: 14 access, 6 deletion, and 3 correction requests. Two are due within 5 days. Each one reached her as a direct message that names the request and links to it, with no personal data in it.

fields.howto_title: How to Build a DSAR Workflow
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to plan the deadlines and reviewers in a DSAR workflow before you build it with Emergent.
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Choose how the app confirms identity
fields.howto_step_1_des: List each system that holds personal data about customers and staff, including the email platform and the HR files. Next to each, write who owns it and the field you search by: an email address or an employee ID.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Write down the request types you accept, such as access and deletion, and the response window your privacy team sets for each law it follows. The app turns each window into a due date the moment a request arrives.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Decide how the app checks that a requester is who they say: a match against the customer record, or a code sent to the email on file. Name who handles a mismatch and what extra detail they may ask the requester for.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Describe the systems in your prompt, and Emergent connects the app to each one through its API. A search returns the records that match the requester, and each delete task goes to the owner you named in the first step.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Name a reviewer for every package
fields.howto_step_5_des: Pick who approves each package before it leaves: a privacy analyst for customer requests, and employment counsel for staff. Require a note with every approval, and keep the package locked until that reviewer signs off.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Choose how many days a system owner can leave a task open before a reminder goes out, and how close to the due date a request moves to the privacy lead. Alerts point to the request and hold no personal data.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Before real requests arrive, run 10 test requests. Make one an employee file and another a request whose identity check fails. Have your privacy team check each due date and approval, and change the rules by prompting until they agree.

faq_plan.a: A DSAR workflow is the set of steps a business runs each time a person asks what data it holds on them, or asks for that data to be deleted or corrected. DSAR stands for data subject access request. The workflow logs the request, checks identity, gathers the data, has a person review it, and sends the reply before the due date.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a DSAR workflow?
faq_plan.a: List the systems that hold personal data and who owns each one, then set a due date rule for each request type. Describe the searches and reviewers in a prompt, and Emergent's AI automation builder builds the app and its database. Run test requests with your privacy team before the first real one arrives.

faq_plan.q: Which steps of a data request can DSAR automation handle?
faq_plan.a: The repeatable steps: logging each request with its due date, searching connected systems and sending delete tasks, then reminding owners who have not replied. A person still decides on identity mismatches and on what gets released. In an app Emergent builds, each of those decisions is saved with the request in a database you own.

faq_plan.q: What due date should a DSAR workflow set for an access request?
faq_plan.a: One month from receipt, for a request under GDPR. A controller acts "without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt of the request," in the words of Article 12. The same article says "That period may be extended by two further months where necessary," and your privacy counsel decides when that applies. The app sets each due date from the window you choose.

faq_plan.q: What due date should a DSAR workflow set for a deletion request?
faq_plan.a: Forty-five calendar days from receipt, under the CCPA regulations. A business responds "no later than 45 calendar days after receipt of the request" and, within 10 business days, "a business shall confirm receipt of the request" too. It "may take up to an additional 45 calendar days" with notice and an explanation, "for a maximum total of 90 calendar days" in all.

faq_plan.q: Does the DSAR workflow clock start before identity is verified?
faq_plan.a: Yes. "The 45-day period will begin on the day that the business receives the request, regardless of time required to verify the request," say the CCPA regulations. Run the identity check early in the workflow. Time spent verifying still counts against the 45 days.

faq_plan.q: What goes into the response package a DSAR workflow sends?
faq_plan.a: A copy of the person's data, gathered from every system that holds it. "The controller shall provide a copy of the personal data undergoing processing," GDPR Article 15 says. What else goes in, and what gets redacted, is your privacy counsel's call. The workflow collects the records so the reviewer starts from one package.

faq_plan.q: How does a DSAR workflow verify who is making the request?
faq_plan.a: It compares what the requester gives with what you hold, such as the name and email on the customer record, or it sends a code to the email on file. Under GDPR Article 12, the controller "may request the provision of additional information necessary to confirm the identity of the data subject" from the requester. A mismatch goes to an analyst, who asks for that detail.

faq_plan.q: Can a DSAR workflow handle requests from employees as well as customers?
faq_plan.a: Yes. An employee request runs through the same steps, but the searches cover HR files and payroll instead of the CRM. Give staff requests their own type and route them to a different reviewer, such as employment counsel, before anything is released. Emergent builds both request types into the same app from your prompt.

faq_plan.q: How do you keep personal data out of DSAR workflow alerts?
faq_plan.a: Keep each alert to the request ID and a link to open it. The reviewer opens the request inside the app, where the records stay in a database you own. The app sends reminders and escalations by Slack or email, in the wording you set.

plan.angle: The pages that rank for this term are privacy-vendor guides that list DSAR steps (receive, verify, collect, review, respond) and sell a privacy platform. This page shows the request-handling app a privacy team builds around those steps: an intake form that opens a numbered request with its due date, identity checks against the customer record, data pulled from the CRM, support desk and billing through their APIs, a named reviewer who approves the package before anything is sent, and a board of every open request by due date. Alerts carry the request number, type and due date with a link, never the person's data. Deadlines are quoted from GDPR Article 12 and the CCPA regulations; the page gives no legal advice, and the privacy team sets every rule.
